title: Create the vault: choose a passphrase
summary: The first time the app starts with no vault, it asks you to choose a passphrase (step 1 of 4). The passphrase opens the vault on this machine; nothing is created anywhere else. Nothing in this version can recover a lost passphrase.
where: App: first run, step 1 of 4. CLI: credmgr init
steps: Type a passphrase of at least 4 characters (8 or more is recommended).
Type it again to confirm.
Choose Next.

title: Recovery code, shown once
summary: Step 2 shows a 256-bit root recovery code once. Together with your passphrase it resets the second factor if you lose your authenticator. Write it on paper and keep it away from the passphrase. Retyping it is optional in the app; the CLI requires the retype before it writes anything.
where: App: first run, step 2 of 4. CLI: credmgr init (retype when asked)
steps: Copy the code onto paper.
Optionally retype it to prove you have it, or skip.
Choose Next.

title: Optional second factor at first run
summary: Step 3 offers to set up a second factor (an authenticator app). The QR code is drawn inside the window and nothing is sent anywhere. After you confirm one code, ten one-time recovery codes are shown once. You may skip it and enrol later in Settings; until you do, the vault rests on the passphrase alone.
where: App: first run, step 3 of 4 (Enrol later to skip)
steps: Scan the QR code, or type the key by hand.
Enter one 6-digit code to confirm.
Save the ten recovery codes, then continue.

title: Name your first projects
summary: Step 4 creates up to three starting projects. Global is created automatically, and so is the Orphaned node that sealing needs. Each project is its own boundary: what is stored in one is invisible to the others. A new vault starts empty; nothing is imported.
where: App: first run, step 4 of 4
steps: Type up to three project names, or leave them blank.
Finish. You land on the graph.

title: The broker is not running
summary: If the app shows 'credmgr cannot reach its broker', the credmgrd process is not running or its socket is not where the app looks. Start credmgrd in a terminal or let launchd keep it running, then choose Retry. Nothing from the last session is shown.
where: App: startup screen. Terminal: credmgrd
steps: Run credmgrd, or install the launchd unit from the release package.
Choose Retry.

title: Unlock with your passphrase
summary: The Lock screen asks for the passphrase. Wrong tries count toward a back-off that grows with each failure; while backed off, the broker answers rate_limited with the seconds to wait.
where: App: Lock screen > passphrase. CLI: credmgr unlock
steps: Type the passphrase.
Press Enter or choose Unlock.
If two-factor is on, the screen asks for a code next.

title: Unlock with a second-factor code
summary: When the vault has a second factor, unlocking asks for the 6 digits from your authenticator, or one of your ten recovery codes (each works once). On the command line, credmgr unlock answers two_factor_required and credmgr gate verify completes it; it asks for the code at a prompt or reads it from stdin, so it never appears in the process list.
where: App: Lock screen > 2FA code. CLI: credmgr gate verify
steps: Enter the 6-digit code or a recovery code.
Choose Verify.

title: Lock the vault now
summary: Locking ends every login, clears a copied secret from the clipboard and returns the app to the Lock screen. It works from anywhere, including while typing or with a dialog open.
where: App: header lock chip, vault menu > Lock vault, or the shortcut Cmd+L. CLI: credmgr lock
steps: Press Cmd+L, or choose the 'unlocked' chip in the header.

title: Auto-lock after idle time
summary: The app locks itself after a period with no activity: 5, 15 or 60 minutes, or never (the setting warns). Even when set to never, the broker still locks on its own idle timer (15 minutes by default). Hiding the window also locks when auto-lock is on.
where: App: Settings > Security > Auto-lock
steps: Open Settings (the gear in the header).
Choose Security.
Pick a time in Auto-lock.

title: Lock on sleep, screen lock and window close
summary: The desktop app locks the vault when the Mac sleeps, when the screen locks, when another user session takes over, and when you close the window. The Lock screen says why it locked. A daemon running without the app does not do this.
where: App: automatic. Menu-bar icon > Lock vault locks on demand
steps: Nothing to do; it happens by itself.
The Lock screen shows a note such as 'Locked because this Mac went to sleep.'

title: Lock a single node
summary: A node can be locked on its own while the vault stays unlocked. Names and types stay visible but values need the node unlocked. A node's policy can lock it after a number of idle seconds.
where: App: node right-click or the three-dot menu > Lock now / Unlock node; inspector > Unlock node. CLI: node policy --lock-after-seconds
steps: Right-click the node, choose Lock now.
To reopen it, choose Unlock node.

title: Unlock a single node
summary: Reopens a node that was locked on its own (by hand or by its idle timer) without touching the rest of the vault. Names and types are visible while it is locked; values and field labels need it unlocked. If a node says it is locked, this is the fix. There is no CLI command for it yet; use the app.
where: App: node menu > Unlock node; inspector > Unlock node
steps: Right-click the node, choose Unlock node.

title: The graph
summary: The main view draws your nodes as a graph. A filled circle is global, a ringed circle a project, a thinner ring a sub-node, a dashed ring the Orphaned node. Small dots around a node are its entries; their colour is a hash of the entry id, never a name or value. You can drag nodes to arrange them; positions are remembered on this device under hashed ids.
where: App: main area, graph mode (the 'graph' button in the left rail)
steps: Click a node to select it and open the inspector.
Drag a node to move it.
Press F to fit the graph to the window.

title: Hover cards
summary: Hovering a node shows how many entries it holds and how many of them are authenticator seeds. Hovering an entry dot shows its entry type. Nothing about names or values.
where: App: hover over a node or an entry dot on the graph
steps: Point at a node.

title: The tree view
summary: The tree is a full keyboard- and screen-reader-accessible peer to the graph, with the same information and the same node menu. It is not a fallback.
where: App: 'tree' button in the left rail, or press T
steps: Press T to switch between graph and tree.
Use the three-dot button on a row for the node menu.

title: The left rail
summary: The rail lists every node with its badges and entry count, plus the Orphaned node. On a narrow window it is hidden behind the menu button (three lines) in the header. Right-click a row for the node menu.
where: App: left rail (the menu button opens it on a narrow window)
steps: Click a row to select the node.
Right-click a row for Open, New entry, Rename, Lock and more.

title: The node menu
summary: Right-clicking a node (or the three-dot button in the tree) offers Open, New entry, New project or New sub-node, Grant access, Rename, Lock now or Unlock node, and Remove node. Global has no Rename or Remove. The Orphaned node only offers Open.
where: App: right-click a node in the graph or rail; three-dot button in the tree
steps: Right-click the node.
Choose an item.

title: Search
summary: The header search box finds node names in the page and entry names through the broker's search. It matches names only: field labels and values are never searched. It shows up to nine rows and says how many more there are. With an empty box it offers 'Add new' and, in Pro mode, recent nodes. A number (1042 or #1042) is also looked up as an entry's reference. The rail has its own filter that narrows the node list by name without asking the broker.
where: App: header search box, or press / to focus it. CLI: credmgr search <term>
steps: Press / (or click the box) and type.
Choose a row to select the node or open the entry.
To narrow the node list instead, type in filter nodes at the top of the rail.

title: Entries: all nodes or selected only
summary: The graph can show every node's entry dots at once or only the selected node's. The choice is remembered.
where: App: button at the top of the graph, or press E
steps: Press E to toggle.

title: The Orphaned node
summary: Orphaned holds sealed items. Names stay visible. A value opens only in the app, one item at a time, after Touch ID and a fresh second factor (when one is on); no agent, command or MCP tool can open it. Without Touch ID set up, the open is refused and the app says how to set it up.
where: App: left rail > orphaned, or vault menu > Orphaned
steps: Select orphaned in the rail.
Read the list of names.
Choose Open on an item and approve Touch ID.

title: Create a project
summary: A project is a boundary: it has its own key, notes and agent scope, and projects never read each other. The dialog takes a name, a parent and optional work folders. In Pro mode an advanced block sets agent access, second-factor requirement, hidden name and sibling sharing at creation.
where: App: right-click global > New project; Settings > Nodes > + New project (Pro); the empty-graph button. CLI: credmgr node create
steps: Open the dialog from one of the places above.
Type a name (1 to 120 characters).
Pick the parent: global makes a project.
Choose Create node.

title: Create a sub-node
summary: A sub-node lives under a project. The tree stops at two levels, so a sub-node cannot have children.
where: App: right-click a project > New sub-node
steps: Right-click the project.
Choose New sub-node.
Name it and choose Create node.

title: Work folders: scope an agent to a node
summary: Binding folders to a node means any process started inside one of them, such as an AI coding agent, is scoped to that node automatically: it can read the node and its ancestors, never another project. The longest matching folder wins. An agent started outside every bound folder sees only that the vault exists.
where: App: New node dialog > work folders. CLI: credmgr node workdir <id> <dir>...
steps: Add a folder when creating the node, or run credmgr node workdir <id> <dir>.
Run credmgr node workdir <id> with no folder to clear the list.

title: Rename a node
summary: Renaming changes the display name only; the node id never changes. Global cannot be renamed.
where: App: right-click a node > Rename, then Enter or click away. CLI: credmgr node rename
steps: Choose Rename, type the new name, press Enter. Esc cancels.

title: Node policy: agent access
summary: Sets what an agent scoped to this node may do: read-write (list, read metadata, reveal, create, update), read-only (list, read metadata, reveal) or none. In the app it is chosen when the node is created (Pro mode); change it later with the CLI.
where: App: New node dialog > advanced (Pro). CLI: credmgr node policy
steps: Run credmgr node policy <id> --reason "why" --agent-access read-only.

title: Node policy: require a second factor
summary: With a vault second factor set up, a node can ask callers other than you for a fresh code: 'reveal' asks before a value leaves the vault, 'always' asks before any read of the node. Your own login is not asked. The factor and the five-minute window belong to the whole vault, not to one node.
where: App: New node dialog > advanced (Pro); the node shows a chip when it is set. CLI: credmgr node policy --require-two-factor
steps: Run credmgr node policy <id> --reason "why" --require-two-factor reveal.

title: Node policy: hide the node's name
summary: A node with hidden names shows other callers an opaque row instead of its label, entry names and notes. The node id is opaque and fixed when the node is created.
where: App: New node dialog > 'Hide this node's name' (Pro). CLI: credmgr node policy --private-names
steps: Tick the option when creating the node, or run credmgr node policy <id> --reason "why" --private-names.

title: Node policy: sibling and descendant reading
summary: Two options widen who can read: sub-nodes seeing each other (siblings shared) and a node reading its children. Turning either off is immediate. Turning either on needs a Touch ID proof (a person present): the command asks for it itself, and with no Touch ID set up the broker refuses and applies nothing.
where: CLI: credmgr node policy --sibling-visibility, --descendant-read
steps: Run credmgr node policy with --sibling-visibility isolated or --no-descendant-read to narrow.
Run it with --sibling-visibility shared or --descendant-read to widen, and approve Touch ID.

title: Node policy: lock a node after idle seconds
summary: A node can carry its own idle timer. When it runs out the node locks while the vault stays open.
where: CLI: credmgr node policy --lock-after-seconds <n>|none
steps: Run credmgr node policy <id> --reason "why" --lock-after-seconds 600.

title: Node notes
summary: Each node can hold one markdown note, sealed under the node's key. The inspector shows it. Writing a note is a CLI action; an empty input is refused so a failed pipe cannot erase a note, and 'notes clear' is the only deletion. Agents never hold the notes capability.
where: App: inspector > notes (read). CLI: credmgr notes show | set | clear
steps: Run credmgr notes set <id> --file ./notes.md.
Run credmgr notes show <id>.

title: Write or clear a node note
summary: Notes are written on the command line: credmgr notes set takes the text from a file or stdin and refuses empty input, and credmgr notes clear is the only way to delete one. The desktop app shows a note but has no editor for it.
where: CLI: credmgr notes set <id> [--file <path>], credmgr notes clear <id>
steps: Run credmgr notes set acme --file ./notes.md.

title: Move a node under a different parent
summary: Re-parenting changes which nodes can read a node, which is a grant by another name, so it needs Admin, a reason and a Touch ID proof (the command asks for it itself). A cycle, Global and Orphaned are refused. With no Touch ID set up the broker refuses. The app has no control for it.
where: CLI: credmgr node reparent <id> --to <parent> --reason "...". No control in the app
steps: Run credmgr node reparent <id> --to <parent> --reason "...".
Approve Touch ID.

title: Add an entry
summary: An entry is one named secret that can hold any number of fields, each with a label you choose. The dialog asks where (which node), a name (up to 200 characters), and either a single set of fields or a bulk paste. A preview shows exactly what will be stored; nothing is written until you save. If the node or vault is locked the entry is held for review instead (see Writes made while locked).
where: App: inspector > + New entry, press N, node menu > New entry, or search > Add new. CLI: credmgr set <name> --node <id>
steps: Press N.
Pick the node and type a name.
Enter label and value, or switch to Bulk.
Check the preview, then choose Save (or Save and add another).

title: Bulk paste: one entry from many lines
summary: Bulk mode takes a paste of 'label: value' lines (a colon followed by a space) and turns it into one entry with one field per line. A line of three slashes separates blocks, so a value can span lines, such as a private key. A box can split each slash-separated block into its own entry. The preview shows the result before you save.
where: App: Add entry dialog > Bulk. CLI: credmgr set <name> --node <id> --bulk
steps: Choose Bulk.
Paste the text.
Check the preview, optionally tick 'split each /// segment into its own entry', then save.

title: Entry type and sensitivity
summary: Every entry has a type (server, database, api, wallet, login, ssh, certificate, token, totp, env-bundle, note or other) and a sensitivity (low, medium, high, critical). Both are inferred from the fields and can be pinned; 'auto' returns to inferring. A seed phrase or private key raises sensitivity to critical.
where: App: Add entry dialog > entry type; preview shows the inferred sensitivity
steps: Leave 'auto', or pick a type in the entry type list.

title: Add a note (free-text entry)
summary: A note is an entry whose single value is free text, for anything that is not a credential. It is audited like any entry. It is different from the node note, which is one markdown page per node.
where: App: inspector > + New note
steps: Select a node.
Choose + New note.
Type the text and save.

title: List the entries of a node
summary: The inspector lists a node's entries with their type and a 2FA badge. A node you cannot read, or one that is locked, says so instead of showing an empty list.
where: App: select a node; inspector on the right. CLI: credmgr list [--node <id>]
steps: Click the node.
Read the list.

title: Open an entry and see its fields
summary: Opening an entry shows its fields: label, type, and a masked value. The broker answers with field ids, labels, types and masking and never a value; values appear only when you reveal or copy one. Labels are encrypted with the values, so a locked node shows only names and types.
where: App: click an entry in the inspector. CLI: credmgr field ls <name>
steps: Click the entry name.
Use the back arrow to return to the node.

title: Replace a value
summary: Replaces one field's value, or the whole field list, in place. It keeps no history. Use rotate when the old value should be kept.
where: CLI: credmgr set <name> --node <id> --field <label>. App: field menu > Edit
steps: Pipe the new value on stdin: credmgr set vps --node acme --field password.

title: Set an expiry date
summary: Gives an entry an expiry date, or removes it. The date is a calendar day in UTC and is metadata: the sealed value is not touched, and nothing is locked or deleted when the day passes. The entry detail shows a chip with the date, amber within 30 days and red once it has passed.
where: App: entry detail > Set expiry… (or Change expiry…). CLI: credmgr expire <name> --node <id> (--at <date> | --in <days> | --clear)
steps: In the app, open the entry and choose Set expiry…, type a date as YYYY-MM-DD or pick in 30 days, in 90 days or in a year, and choose Save expiry.
To remove it, choose Change expiry… and then Remove expiry.
On the command line, run credmgr expire stripe --node acme --in 90 to expire it in 90 days, or --clear to remove the date.

title: Edit an entry's details in your editor
summary: Opens an entry's details (aliases, expiry, sensitivity, type, tags when offered, and each field's label, type and masking) as a small text file in your editor, then applies only the lines you changed. No secret value is in the file and none can be changed there; renaming is not supported. Nothing is applied if a line is malformed.
where: CLI: credmgr edit <name> --node <id> [--dry-run]
steps: Run credmgr edit stripe --node acme. Your editor opens (VISUAL, then EDITOR, then vi) on a private temporary file.
Change the lines you want and save. Lines you leave alone change nothing.
Add --dry-run to see what would be applied without applying it. If the entry changed meanwhile, your edited file is kept and its path is printed so you can retry.

title: Entries about to expire
summary: Lists the entries whose expiry falls within the next N days (30 unless you say), soonest first, including any already expired. Names and dates only, never a value. Human sessions only.
where: CLI: credmgr expiring [--days N] [--node <id>]
steps: Run credmgr expiring to see the next 30 days, or add --days 90.

title: Move an entry to another project
summary: Moves one entry to another project (node). The value is sealed again with that project's key inside the broker, in one step that survives a crash: the entry is never readable in both projects and never lost. Its name, other names, expiry and reference number go with it. Grants on the entry are revoked and earlier values kept for Undo are dropped. A name the other project already uses is refused. Your login only, with a fresh second-factor code when one is set up and Touch ID every time; no agent can move an entry.
where: App: entry detail > Move to project…. CLI: credmgr move <name> --node <id> --to <id>
steps: In the app, open the entry, choose Move to project…, pick the project and choose Move entry. Touch ID is asked for.
On the command line, run credmgr move stripe --node acme --to billing.
If the other project already has an entry with that name or one of its other names, rename one of them first.

title: An entry's history
summary: Shows one entry's trail: every audit record that names it (created, changed, rotated, revealed, denied), oldest first, and when it was last rotated and edited. Values are never in the audit log, so none is shown. Human sessions only. The app shows the newest 200 records, newest first, on the entry's History tab.
where: App: entry detail > History. CLI: credmgr history <name> [--node <id>] [--limit N]
steps: In the app, open the entry and choose the History tab; Refresh reads it again.
On the command line, run credmgr history stripe --node acme.

title: Find an entry by its number
summary: Every entry has a short reference number that is unique across the vault. This finds the entry it belongs to, among the entries you could already list; a number in a node you cannot reach answers not found, the same as no such number.
where: App: type the number (1042 or #1042) in the header search box. CLI: credmgr ref <number>
steps: In the app, type the number in the search box; the entry it names comes first. Choose it to open the entry.
On the command line, run credmgr ref 1042.

title: Search one node
summary: Finds names and aliases containing a word on one node, case-insensitive. Names only, never values. The header search box and credmgr search search the whole vault instead.
where: App: select a node; Find in this node, above its entries. Broker operation entry.search (no command of its own)
steps: Select the node in the rail.
Type in Find in this node; a match on another name says which.
Choose a result to open the entry.

title: Rotate a secret and keep history
summary: Rotation replaces a value and keeps the previous one as history, so it can be undone with no time limit, and the entry records when it was rotated. A legitimate rotation implies you could have read what you replace, so it needs the vault unlocked.
where: App: entry detail > Rotate…. CLI: credmgr rotate <name>
steps: In the app, open the entry and choose Rotate…, pick the field (the hidden one is chosen first), type the new value or choose Generate, and choose Rotate. Undo under the fields puts the old value back.
On the command line, pipe the new value on stdin: credmgr rotate API_KEY --node acme.

title: Remove an entry (soft delete)
summary: Removing hides the entry from lists and search at once and keeps it, sealed, for seven days, when Undo can bring it back. After seven days it is deleted for good.
where: App: entry detail > Remove…, then Undo in the node's list or Restore in Settings > Audit. CLI: credmgr rm <name>
steps: In the app, open the entry, choose Remove… and confirm with Remove entry.
To bring it back, choose Undo on the bar in the node's list, or Restore under removed in the last 7 days in Settings > Audit. If another entry has taken the name, choose Restore as a copy.
On the command line, run credmgr rm <name> --node <id>, and credmgr undo <audit id> --node <id> to bring it back inside seven days.

title: Undo a change
summary: Undo reverses a rotation, a field change or a removal, addressed by the audit record id. A removal can be undone for seven days and a field change for seven days; a rotation has no limit. In the app the inspector shows 'Undo' for the most recent change on the node while nothing else has changed it. Undo is itself an audited action.
where: App: inspector > Undo button under the fields. CLI: credmgr undo <audit id> --node <id>
steps: Find the id with credmgr audit, then run credmgr undo <id> --node <node>.
If the name was reused, add --mode keep-both.

title: Generate a password
summary: The broker can generate a random password of 8 to 128 characters, with symbols on or off, a pronounceable form, or lower-case hex only (--hex), and tells you its strength. On the command line, --copy puts the value on the macOS clipboard instead of stdout and clears it after 30 seconds if it is unchanged. The value appears in the answer only; it is not stored or audited until you save it in a field.
where: App: Add field dialog > Generate. CLI: credmgr generate
steps: Open + Add field.
Set the length and options.
Choose Generate, then save the field.

title: Entry and node name rules
summary: Names are compared in one canonical form, so a look-alike of an existing name (different case, width, invisible characters or look-alike letters) is refused as already existing, for agents too. A name that mixes Latin with Greek or Cyrillic letters is accepted with a warning. Entry names are at most 200 characters; node labels 1 to 120.
where: Applies wherever a name is typed
steps: Choose a different name if you see 'already exists'.

title: Add a field
summary: Adds one or more fields to an entry, appended or inserted at a position. The label is free text and may be empty; there are no fixed field names. The type and whether it is hidden are inferred from the label and value.
where: App: open an entry > + Add field. CLI: credmgr field add
steps: Open the entry.
Choose + Add field.
Type a label and a value (or Generate), then save.

title: Edit a field
summary: Changes a field's label, value, type or hidden state. The current value is never shown in the dialog; leave the new value empty to keep it. Only what you change is sent. The previous state is kept as history.
where: App: field three-dot menu > Edit. CLI: credmgr field set
steps: Open the field menu and choose Edit.
Change what you need and save.

title: Remove a field
summary: Removes one field from an entry. An entry keeps at least one field; remove the entry instead. Undoable.
where: App: field three-dot menu > Remove. CLI: credmgr field rm
steps: Open the field menu, choose Remove, confirm.

title: Reorder fields
summary: Moves a field up or down. Order is presentation only.
where: App: field three-dot menu > Move up / Move down. CLI: credmgr field mv
steps: Open the field menu and choose Move up or Move down.

title: Field types and hidden values
summary: A field has one of eleven types: password, api-key, private-key, seed-phrase, totp-seed, username, host, port, url, certificate, text. The type is inferred from label and value and can be pinned. Password, api-key, private-key, seed-phrase and totp-seed fields are hidden by default; any field can be pinned shown or hidden.
where: App: Add entry preview and Edit field dialog
steps: Pick a type in the preview list, or choose auto.

title: Reveal a value
summary: Reveal fetches one field's value and shows it for the reveal window (10, 20 or 60 seconds; 20 by default), then hides it again with a countdown. Each reveal is audited. An agent asking the broker for a value goes through the same gate: if the vault is locked the request waits for you; if the node asks for a second factor it needs a fresh code.
where: App: open an entry > Reveal on a field. CLI: credmgr get <name> --field <label>
steps: Open the entry.
Choose Reveal on the field.
The value hides again when the countdown ends or you lock.

title: Copy a value without revealing it
summary: Copy places the value on the clipboard through the app's native shell and never passes it through the window. The clipboard is cleared after 30 seconds and when the vault locks. Every copy is audited.
where: App: field row > Copy
steps: Choose Copy on the field.
Paste within 30 seconds.

title: Read a value on the command line
summary: credmgr get prints one value on stdout. An entry with several fields needs a selector (--field, --field-id) or --all; without one it exits 2 and lists the labels. --json prints the fields. --copy puts one value on the macOS clipboard instead of stdout (cleared after 30 seconds if unchanged).
where: CLI: credmgr get
steps: credmgr get API_KEY --node acme
credmgr get vps --node acme --field password

title: Conflict protection on writes
summary: Every change to an existing entry carries the entry's current generation. If something else changed it first, the broker answers conflict with both generations and nothing is applied. Re-read, re-apply, retry once.
where: Automatic
steps: On a conflict, read the entry again and repeat the change.

title: Store an authenticator seed
summary: A field holding an otpauth URI, a base32 secret of a standard length (16, 20, 24, 26, 32, 40, 52, 56 or 64 characters, upper case or in groups of four), or a field typed totp-seed is a stored authenticator seed. The entry gets a 2FA badge and counts toward the node's 2FA number. This is separate from the vault's own second factor.
where: App: Add entry with a seed field. CLI: credmgr set <name> --node <id>
steps: Add a field whose value is the seed.
The entry shows a 2FA badge.

title: Import an authenticator seed from a QR image
summary: In Add entry, drop a PNG or JPEG of an authenticator QR code on the 2FA QR box, or choose one. The image is read on this computer, never uploaded or saved, and the otpauth URI in it goes into a field as if you had pasted it; the preview types it a 2FA seed. A QR code that is not an authenticator code is refused. Nothing is stored until you save.
where: App: Add entry > 2FA QR
steps: Open Add entry in a project.
Drop the QR image on the 2FA QR box, or choose the file.
Name the entry and save.

title: Show the current 6-digit code
summary: Revealing a seed field shows the current 6-digit code with a bar that runs to the end of its 30-second step. A reveal of a seed field never returns the seed, only the code; the seed has its own Touch ID-gated 'show seed'. Codes use SHA-1, 6 digits, 30 seconds.
where: App: seed field > Reveal. CLI: credmgr totp <name>. MCP: credmgr_totp_code
steps: Open the entry.
Choose Reveal on the seed field.

title: Show the seed itself
summary: A code is worth thirty seconds, a seed is worth forever. The broker releases a seed only to the owner's login with a Touch ID proof and never to an agent. In the app, 'show seed' asks for your fingerprint and then shows the seed in that field's row for the reveal window, like a revealed value: it re-masks by itself, is wiped when the vault locks or the window is hidden, and can never be copied. Without Touch ID set up, or if you cancel the prompt, nothing is shown and the notice says how to set Touch ID up. There is no CLI command for it.
where: App: seed field > show seed (asks for Touch ID, then shows the seed for the reveal window)
steps: Set up Touch ID in Settings > Security if you have not.
Open the entry and choose show seed on the seed field.
Confirm with your fingerprint; the seed shows until it re-masks.

title: Set up or replace the second factor
summary: Enrolling gives the vault a second factor: the broker will not unlock without a fresh code from your authenticator. The QR code is drawn locally. After you confirm one code, ten recovery codes are shown once. Replacing a confirmed factor needs a fresh code from the current one first (unlock again, then do it within five minutes).
where: App: Settings > Security > Two-factor gate. CLI: credmgr gate enroll
steps: Choose Enrol (or Replace).
Scan the QR code and enter one code.
Save the ten recovery codes.

title: Lost your authenticator
summary: The passphrase, plus the root recovery code printed when the vault was created, resets the second factor. It does not unlock: unlock afterwards, then enrol a new authenticator. Without both, nothing recovers it.
where: App: Lock screen > 'lost your authenticator?'. CLI: credmgr gate recover
steps: Choose 'lost your authenticator?'.
Enter the passphrase and the root recovery code.
Choose Reset and unlock, then enrol again.

title: The ten recovery codes
summary: Enrolment issues ten one-time codes, each good once in place of an authenticator code at unlock. They are shown once and cannot be shown again. They are not the root recovery code.
where: App: after confirming a code; the Lock screen accepts one in the 2FA field
steps: Store them apart from the passphrase.

title: Give the second factor to agents
summary: For nodes whose policy asks for a second factor, an agent or tool gets two_factor_required until a person proves the factor. One code opens a vault-wide window of five minutes in which agents and other tools pass the gate on every node that asks. A lock or any node policy change ends it. Your own login is never asked.
where: App: 'Give second factor' on the node chip or in the inspector. CLI: credmgr gate verify in a shell that holds your login
steps: Choose Give second factor on the node.
Enter the current authenticator code.

title: What the second factor does and does not protect
summary: The check is made by credmgrd, not by the encryption. Anyone who has your passphrase or your recovery code and a copy of the vault folder can decrypt it without the second factor. Treat each of the passphrase and the recovery code as a complete key.
where: Applies to the whole vault
steps: Keep the passphrase and recovery code offline and apart.

title: Decide an agent's waiting request
summary: If an agent asks for a value while the whole vault is locked, the broker records the request and answers approval_pending. You decide it while the vault stays locked: you give the passphrase (and the authenticator code if two-factor is on). On the command line the passphrase is the first stdin line and the code the second, or it is asked for at a terminal. Approving decrypts that one entry and hands it to the agent's retry once; the vault stays locked. A request expires and is denied after 120 seconds.
where: App: Lock screen > 'N agent requests are waiting for approval'. CLI: credmgr approvals, credmgr approve <request>
steps: Open the Lock screen's request list and pick a request.
Enter the passphrase (and code).
Choose Approve or Deny.

title: See what a request asks for
summary: Before deciding, you can see what each waiting request is: the node, the entry (by name unless the node hides names), the command and the seconds left. The list works while locked and decrypts nothing. The Lock screen checks the waiting count every five seconds.
where: App: Lock screen request list. CLI: credmgr approvals [<request>]
steps: Run credmgr approvals, or open the request list on the Lock screen.

title: Writes made while locked are held for review
summary: An entry added while the vault or its node is locked does not enter the manifest. It waits in the pending tray, across restarts, showing node, name, field count, type, sensitivity and when it was held, and never its values. Accept writes it to its node; Discard removes it. Accepting needs the node unlocked.
where: App: header 'N held' chip, the banner after unlock (Review), or vault menu > Pending writes. CLI: credmgr pending
steps: Open Held for review.
Choose Accept or Discard on each row.

title: Accept or discard a held entry
summary: Each held entry is accepted or discarded on its own. A name already used on the node is refused rather than overwritten.
where: App: Held for review > Accept / Discard. CLI: credmgr pending accept|discard <entry> --node <id>
steps: credmgr pending accept <entry> --node acme.

title: The review banner
summary: After you unlock, a banner reports how many held entries are waiting, with Review and dismiss buttons. The header chip stays until the tray is empty.
where: App: banner under the header after unlock
steps: Choose Review.

title: See and revoke grants
summary: A grant lets one node see into another. The list shows from and to, the scope (read, reveal, notes), a reason and when it ends. Revoking closes it at once in both Lite and Pro mode, because revoking is safety.
where: App: Settings > Grants > Revoke. CLI: credmgr grant ls, credmgr grant revoke <id>
steps: Open Settings > Grants.
Choose Revoke on the row.

title: List grants
summary: Shows every grant: from and to, scope, reason and when it ends. Grants made elsewhere appear here even though this build cannot create one.
where: App: Settings > Grants. CLI: credmgr grant ls
steps: Open Settings > Grants, or run credmgr grant ls.

title: Create a grant
summary: The dialog takes a from-node, a to-node, what to allow (read, reveal values, notes) and a reason of at least eight characters. Creating a grant widens a boundary, so it asks for Touch ID and then writes the grant; with no Touch ID set up the broker refuses with presence_required and nothing changes. Grants made elsewhere are listed and can be revoked. A grant never expires by itself.
where: App: node menu > Grant access; Settings > Grants > + New grant (Pro); drag one node onto another. CLI: credmgr grant <from> --to <node> --scope read --reason "..."
steps: The dialog validates your input, asks for Touch ID and shows the result.

title: How isolation and grants work
summary: Projects never read each other. A node reads itself, Global and its ancestors. It reads its children only if its own policy allows it, and a sibling only for sub-nodes whose parent shares them. Anything else is a grant: human-only, with a reason, revocable, drawn as a dashed arrow on the graph from the trusted node to the node it can see into. An agent can never create one.
where: Concept; see the graph legend in Help
steps: Read the dashed arrows on the graph.

title: Remove (seal) a node
summary: Removing a node never deletes it. Its entries are re-encrypted to the Orphaned node's key, names stay visible and values become human-only. You type the node name to confirm. A node that still has sub-nodes cannot be sealed until they are sealed; Global cannot be sealed.
where: App: node menu > Remove node; Settings > Nodes > Remove (Pro). CLI: credmgr node seal <name>
steps: Choose Remove node.
Type the node name.
Choose Seal node.

title: Restore a sealed node
summary: A sealed node can be restored byte for byte for seven days, across restarts. After that restore is refused (archive_expired). Work folders another node has claimed since are not restored.
where: App: Settings > Nodes > Sealed nodes > Restore node (Pro). CLI: credmgr node restore <name>
steps: Open Settings > Nodes.
Choose Restore node on the sealed row.

title: Destroy expired seals
summary: After seven days a sealed node's retained originals can be destroyed for good. Nothing does this by itself: only credmgr doctor --purge-expired-seals, or the Operations panel's 'Doctor with purge' followed by Apply. A plain Doctor never purges. The Orphaned copies stay encrypted.
where: App: Operations (Cmd+Shift+O) > Doctor with purge. CLI: credmgr doctor --purge-expired-seals
steps: Preview first with --dry-run, then apply.

title: The audit trail
summary: Every request the broker decides, allowed or denied, is recorded in a hash-chained log. The Audit screen lists newest first: time, action, what it touched and who. An agent sees a redacted feed of id, action, time and actor, never values. Audit is a Pro-mode screen.
where: App: Settings > Audit (Pro). CLI: credmgr audit [--limit N]
steps: Open Settings > Audit.
Choose Refresh.

title: Open the full audit record
summary: Clicking a row asks for the full, unredacted record, after Touch ID. The app shows a one-line summary of it. With no Touch ID set up the broker refuses and the app says so.
where: App: Settings > Audit > click a row (asks for Touch ID)
steps: Open Settings > Audit.
Click a row.
Approve Touch ID.

title: Audit report
summary: A 30-day report of denied requests and grant changes.
where: App: Operations (Cmd+Shift+O) > Audit report
steps: Choose Run on the Audit report row.

title: Back up the vault
summary: Writes a complete encrypted archive into the vault's backups folder (while the machine lock is on, into CredMgr's state folder on this Mac instead, outside the vault folder) under a passphrase you choose: entries, notes, sealed-node and removed-entry archives, rotation history, the audit log and the keys, and a restore ticket in place of the rollback counter (which stays on this Mac; the first unlock of the restored vault sets a new one). Restore it from Settings > Restore from backup or with credmgr restore, into an empty directory, while the broker is not running. Take the backup while the vault is idle.
where: App: Settings > Backup > Back up now, or Operations > Back up vault. CLI: credmgr backup [--retain N]
steps: Choose Back up now.
Choose and repeat an archive passphrase.

title: Restore a backup
summary: Rebuilds a vault from a backup archive into an empty folder: the backup passphrase is never on a command line, nothing is merged into or written over an existing vault, and the archive is checked whole before a single file is written. A restore never runs beside a running broker: it is refused while credmgrd answers on the vault's socket, in the app and in the terminal alike (the app runs the same credmgr restore). Afterwards unlock with your vault passphrase and run verify. An existing generation counter on this machine is kept, so an archive older than it is refused as rolled back.
where: App: Settings > Backup > Restore…, or Restore from a backup… on the screen the app shows when no broker answers. CLI: credmgr restore <archive> [--to <empty dir>] [--state-dir <dir>] [--json]
steps: Quit CredMgr, and stop credmgrd if Start at login keeps it running: a restore is refused while a broker runs.
In the app, on the screen it shows when no broker answers, choose Restore from a backup…, give the archive's path, an empty folder and the backup passphrase, and choose Restore.
Or run credmgr restore with the archive file and an empty --to directory; give the backup passphrase on stdin.
Start the broker on that folder, unlock with your vault passphrase, and run credmgr verify.

title: Backup retention
summary: Keeps the 14 or 30 most recent archives. Shown in Pro mode.
where: App: Settings > Backup > Retention (Pro)
steps: Pick 14 or 30 archives.

title: Verify integrity
summary: Checks every envelope against its manifest digest and the registry. Run it after copying or restoring files, or when something looks wrong. The result is ok or a count of problems.
where: App: Settings > Backup > Verify now, or Operations > Verify integrity. CLI: credmgr verify
steps: Choose Verify now.

title: Doctor
summary: Diagnoses registry and manifest problems; a dry run shows what it would fix. It never purges anything on its own. Rebuilding the registry needs a Touch ID proof (and the passphrase of the backup it uses); with no Touch ID set up the broker refuses.
where: App: Operations (Cmd+Shift+O) > Doctor. CLI: credmgr doctor [--dry-run]
steps: Run with --dry-run first.

title: Tidy up (the doctor's scan of your entries)
summary: Scans the vault for entries that share a value, near-identical names, entries in Global named for one project, weak passwords, values stored as the wrong kind (a whole otpauth:// link as a password, a live key in a test project), and entries that are expired, about to expire or not rotated for a year. It never shows a value: shared values are found inside the broker with a key made for that one scan and thrown away after it. It changes nothing. Where moving an entry fixes a finding, Move to <project> opens the entry's Move dialog with that project chosen, and the move asks for Touch ID as always. Nodes it could not read (locked, or waiting for their own second factor) are listed. Your login only; no agent can run it.
where: App: Settings > Maintenance > Tidy up…, or Operations (Cmd+Shift+O) > Tidy up. CLI: credmgr doctor --scan
steps: In the app, open Tidy up and read the findings by kind; each says what to do.
Choose Move to <project> on a finding to move that entry; after the move the scan runs again.
On the command line, run credmgr doctor --scan; add --stale-days 180 or --expiring-days 14 to change the windows, or --json for the report.

title: Apply all the moves Tidy up proposes
summary: Moves every entry Tidy up proposes to move, in one step: the entries in Global named for one project, and one copy of a value two sub-projects of a project share. Before anything moves you see the whole list, each entry with where it comes from and where it goes, and confirm it; exactly that list is sent. One authenticator code (when a second factor is on) and one Touch ID check cover the whole list. Each entry is moved the way Move moves one: re-encrypted to its new project's key, keeping its name, reference and expiry; grants on it are revoked and its Undo history stays behind. If the vault changed since the scan, nothing moves. If a move fails part-way, the moves before it stay made and you are told which ones; move one back with Move. Your login only; no agent can do it.
where: App: Tidy up > Apply all moves. CLI: credmgr doctor --scan --apply
steps: In the app, open Tidy up, press Apply all moves (N), read the list and press Apply.
On the command line, run credmgr doctor --scan --apply, read the plan it prints and answer y; --yes applies the plan shown without asking.
To undo one move, open the entry and Move it back.

title: Rotate the root key
summary: Replaces the root key every other key is wrapped under and issues a new recovery code. It asks for the vault passphrase again, a fresh second factor (when one is on) and Touch ID; with no Touch ID set up the broker refuses and nothing changes. If Touch ID unlock is on it is re-sealed to the same Mac key. The command line has no command for it. A Touch ID unlock set up in 2.0.0-beta.1 (before version 2.0.0-rc.2) must be turned off and on again first: the rotation refuses to seal the new key to an unlock file it cannot authenticate.
where: App: Settings > Advanced > Rotate (Pro), or Operations
steps: Open Settings > Advanced.
Choose Rotate and enter the vault passphrase.
Approve Touch ID (and the second factor).
Save the new recovery code.

title: Change the vault passphrase
summary: Changes the passphrase that opens the vault. It asks for the current passphrase and the new one twice, then replaces the root key under the new passphrase, so it also issues a new recovery code (shown once; the old code stops working). It asks for a fresh second factor when one is on, and Touch ID when a Touch ID key is set up; without Touch ID the current passphrase is the proof it is you. The same passphrase twice is refused.
where: App: Settings > Security > Passphrase > Change. CLI: credmgr passphrase
steps: Open Settings > Security and choose Change on the Passphrase row.
Enter the current passphrase, then the new one twice.
Approve Touch ID and the second factor if asked.
Save the new recovery code.

title: Forgot the passphrase? Open the vault with the recovery code
summary: Opens a locked vault with the recovery code you saved when you created it, when the passphrase is forgotten. In the same step you choose a new passphrase and get a new recovery code (shown once); the code you used and the old passphrase stop working. If a second factor is on it still asks for it (an authenticator code or one of its printed backup codes); Touch ID is not needed. Wrong codes are slowed down like wrong passphrases, and every attempt is in the audit log. An older vault, made before recovery wraps existed, gets the option after its next passphrase change.
where: App: Lock screen > Forgot passphrase? Use recovery code. CLI: credmgr recover
steps: On the Lock screen choose Forgot passphrase? Use recovery code.
Type the recovery code, then a new passphrase twice.
Give the second-factor code if asked.
Save the new recovery code: the old one no longer works.

title: The Operations panel
summary: A Pro-mode panel with Verify integrity, Doctor, Doctor with purge, Back up vault, Rotate root key and Audit report. It shows each result in place.
where: App: vault menu > Operations, or Cmd+Shift+O
steps: Press Cmd+Shift+O.

title: Import a .env file
summary: Turns a .env-style file (NAME=value lines, # comments, export, quotes) into entries. Two ways: credmgr import (one all-or-nothing call; also reads a .json file, or --format json, as an array of name+value or name+fields entries) and credmgr import-env / the window's Import .env... (previews every name first). A missing closing quote names the line, never its content. Values are never printed. Your .env file is not touched.
where: CLI: credmgr import <file|-> --node <id>, credmgr import-env <file|-> --node <id>. App: inspector > Import .env...
steps: credmgr import ./service.env --node acme
Delete the .env yourself once you have checked the result.

title: Open Settings
summary: Settings is a panel with sections. Lite mode shows Security, Appearance, Backup, Mode, Grants and Games. Pro mode (the default) adds Nodes, Maintenance, Audit, Advanced and Operations.
where: App: the gear in the header
steps: Choose the gear.
Pick a section on the left.

title: Lite and Pro mode
summary: Lite hides levers, never safety: backup, integrity checking and revoking a grant are available in both. Pro adds Nodes, creating grants, Maintenance, Audit, Advanced and the Operations panel. Switching is instant and never hides data.
where: App: Settings > Mode
steps: Choose Lite or Pro.

title: Reveal window
summary: How long a revealed value stays visible before it hides again: 10, 20 (default) or 60 seconds.
where: App: Settings > Security > Reveal window
steps: Pick a time.

title: Confirm before showing secrets
summary: Off by default. When it is on, the vault asks you to confirm it is you, with Touch ID or the vault passphrase, before it shows a saved secret: revealing a value, copying one, or showing a one-time code. After you confirm, it does not ask again for the trust window you chose (1, 5, 15 or 60 minutes; 5 by default). Locking the vault ends the trust window. It guards this app and your logged-in command line (credmgr with your login), on a Mac that is left unlocked. It does not ask agents, including a credmgr command run from inside a registered project folder without your login: what they may read is decided by each project's security level. Approving a waiting request asks too, because approving releases a value. The setting is kept in the vault's signed registry. Turning it off, or making it ask less, needs a fresh confirmation; turning it on does not.
where: App: Settings > Security > Confirm before showing secrets. CLI: credmgr confirm
steps: Open Settings > Security.
Turn on Confirm before showing secrets.
Choose how long a confirmation lasts (the trust window).
The next time you show a secret, confirm with Touch ID or your passphrase.

title: Confirm every time, or only for high and critical secrets
summary: In Pro mode, Settings > Security has two more choices for Confirm before showing secrets. When to ask: once per trust window, or every time (each secret needs its own confirmation, so Touch ID asks once per reveal). Which secrets: all of them, or only entries whose sensitivity is high or critical (low and medium values show without asking). Under the second choice, lowering an entry's sensitivity out of high or critical also asks you to confirm. Making the rule ask less needs a fresh confirmation.
where: App: Settings > Security (Pro mode) > When to ask, Which secrets
steps: Switch to Pro in Settings > Mode.
Open Settings > Security.
Under Confirm before showing secrets choose When to ask and Which secrets.

title: Concealed clipboard
summary: Always on and not a choice: a copied secret is cleared after 30 seconds and when the vault locks, and never enters the window.
where: App: Settings > Security > Concealed clipboard (shows 'on')
steps: Nothing to set.

title: Theme, colour, contrast and motion
summary: Dark or light theme; colour off, on or auto with hue and intensity sliders (grounds are tinted, never coloured); standard or high contrast; system or reduced motion; hardware acceleration on or off; a greyscale proof mode for design review.
where: App: Settings > Appearance
steps: Choose the options.

title: Turn single-key shortcuts off
summary: The shortcuts / F G T N E work without a modifier. Turn them off if they get in the way of speech input or a screen reader. Cmd+L and Cmd+Shift+O always work.
where: App: Settings > Appearance > Single-key shortcuts
steps: Choose the button to toggle.

title: Hide the window from screen capture and screen sharing
summary: The window is hidden from screenshots, screen recordings and screen sharing by default. Turn the switch off to allow capture; the app asks you to confirm first and shows a 'capture allowed' chip while it is off. The choice is remembered.
where: App: gear > Security > Hide the window from screen capture and screen sharing
steps: Choose the gear, then Security.
Switch 'Hide the window from screen capture and screen sharing' on or off.
Turning it off asks for confirmation; turning it on does not.

title: Milestones
summary: A private record of your use, kept on this device as dates only, free for everyone.
where: App: Settings > Appearance > Milestones
steps: Read the list.

title: Supporter extras (cosmetic)
summary: Optional cosmetic choices: node shape and colours, backdrop, flourish, ball trail, app mark, the Dock icon, glyph weight, double halo and header badge. They open with a supporter code e-mailed after a donation, once, on this device. Nothing functional is ever locked behind a donation. Some options are badged 'not in beta.1'.
where: App: Settings > Appearance > Supporter extras > Enter code
steps: Choose Enter code and type the code.

title: Donations and the reminder
summary: A donation is a voluntary gift: not refundable, buys no features and gives no influence. About > Donate lists the addresses with a checklist (verify the first and last six characters after pasting; send a small test first). A dismissible reminder appears about six seconds after unlock and can be turned off with 'don't remind me' or a supporter code.
where: App: About > Donate; reminder box after unlock
steps: Open About, choose Donate.
Copy an address and verify it.

title: CredGames
summary: Small local games for Graph mode, starting with CredPong. A game may read how many nodes the vault has and how many entries each holds, never a name, a field or a value. It writes nothing to the vault and has no network. Scores stay on this device.
where: App: vault menu > Games, the rail's games button, or Settings > Games
steps: Open Games and choose Play.

title: Menu-bar icon
summary: The app stays reachable after its window is closed. Left-click the icon to show the window. Right-click (or Ctrl-click) for Open CredMgr, Lock vault and Quit CredMgr. Closing the window hides it and locks the vault; Quit locks it too. Clicking the Dock icon also shows the window.
where: App: macOS menu bar
steps: Right-click the icon for the menu.

title: The MCP server for AI agents
summary: credmgr mcp is a stdio MCP server that exposes 21 tools to an AI client. It forwards each call to the broker unchanged; the broker decides. You register it once, globally, in your AI client's MCP settings with the full path to the credmgr binary and the argument mcp. One entry serves every project because the folder the client starts in decides the node. Settings, Agents shows the exact configuration for each client and writes it only when you press Write on the change it shows; credmgr mcp --print-config prints it for a terminal.
where: Settings, Agents (the app). CLI: credmgr mcp --print-config <client>; credmgr agent connect <client>
steps: Open Settings, Agents, and press Connect on your assistant (or copy the configuration).
Read the change, then press Write this change. Restart the assistant.
Start the assistant inside a project folder bound to a node.

title: An agent learns its own boundary
summary: credmgr_whoami returns the agent's node, its capabilities, the nodes it can reach and the node's security level, and names nothing else. An agent should call it first and reason about its own boundary instead of discovering it by being denied.
where: MCP: credmgr_whoami. CLI: credmgr whoami
steps: Call credmgr_whoami before anything else.

title: How an agent is scoped
summary: An agent is scoped to one node, resolved from the folder it was started in (the node's work folders), or from an explicit token. It reads that node, its ancestors and Global, plus anything granted. No tool argument changes that. An agent started in an unbound folder gets only a bare list on Global.
where: Set with work folders on a node
steps: Bind the project folder to the node (see Work folders).

title: What each agent access level allows
summary: The node's agent access decides the agent's capabilities. read-write: list, read metadata, reveal, create, update. read-only: list, read metadata, reveal. none: nothing. The notes and admin capabilities are never part of an agent's scope, whatever the policy says. The security level (Open, Guarded, Strict) is separate: it decides which of those actions wait for you.
where: CLI: credmgr node policy <id> --reason "..." --agent-access ...
steps: Choose the narrowest level that does the job.

title: What an agent sees when the vault is locked
summary: Reading a value on a locked vault answers approval_pending and waits for you (see Decide an agent's waiting request); asking for an authenticator code on a locked vault is simply refused. Creating an entry works and lands in the pending tray for your review. Updating, rotating, removing and field changes are refused with vault_locked, because overwriting a credential you cannot read would be substitution.
where: Behaviour of the broker
steps: Agent: wait or carry on with other work; do not retry in a loop.

title: What an agent does when refused
summary: A refusal is explicit and names the human action that would fix it in its remedy field. The right response is to say what is needed and why in one sentence, ask the operator, and carry on with other work. Do not retry, rephrase or look for another route.
where: Every MCP tool result that is an error
steps: Read error and remedy.
Tell the operator what you need.

title: What an agent can never do
summary: These are absent, not merely gated: create or change a grant; read the Orphaned node; read a stored authenticator seed (it can get the current 6-digit code); change a node's policy, agent access, name, parent or work folders; touch the second factor or recovery; run backup, verify, doctor or root-key rotation; purge or shorten the audit log or the recovery window; read another node under any argument; read notes. A test fails if a tool for any of these is added.
where: Enforced in the broker; restated in the MCP registry
steps: Ask the operator instead.

title: Private names and agents
summary: On a node with hidden names, an agent sees an opaque row (nameHidden) instead of its label, entry names and notes, and search skips the node.
where: Node policy: private names
steps: Set private names on a sensitive node.

title: Machine-readable manifest for AI agents
summary: v2/docs/llm/credmgr-capabilities.json describes every feature, the 21 MCP tools with their input schemas, the error codes with what to do on each, the broker operations (which ones an agent can reach), the CLI commands and the safety rules. It is generated from the same data as this help and is checked against the code, so it cannot silently drift.
where: File: v2/docs/llm/credmgr-capabilities.json. Regenerate: python3 tools/gen_help.py
steps: Give the file to an agent as context.

title: Keep your login out of an agent's shell
summary: credmgr unlock exports a login token that reaches every project until the vault locks or the token idles out for 15 minutes. Never export it into a shell an AI agent runs in: the agent would inherit your reach. Agents should use the MCP server, scoped by folder, or an agent token for one node. The MCP server never reads CREDMGR_TOKEN and refuses to start if CREDMGR_AGENT_TOKEN holds a login.
where: CLI: credmgr unlock; known risk K-6
steps: Unlock in a shell the agent cannot read, and lock when done.

title: Give an agent a token for one node
summary: An agent token lets an agent reach exactly one project node (not Global), with the capabilities you pick (list, read, reveal, create, update) and never more than that node allows agents. It always expires: one day unless you choose otherwise, seven days at most. Issuing needs your login, your second factor if you set one up, and Touch ID; an agent can never issue, widen or renew one. You get the token once: the app puts it on the clipboard (concealed, cleared after 30 seconds) without showing it, and the CLI prints it alone. Paste it into the agent's settings as CREDMGR_AGENT_TOKEN. Restarting the broker, or sealing the node, ends its agent tokens. When an agent asks for a reveal approval or a setting change with a token, the request says which token asked.
where: App: Settings > Agents > Agent tokens > Issue token. CLI: credmgr agent token issue <node> --label "..." --cap list,read [--expires 8h]
steps: Open Settings > Agents and choose Issue token under Agent tokens.
Pick the node, name the agent, tick what it may do and choose how long the token lasts.
Confirm with Touch ID. The token is now on the clipboard: paste it into the agent's settings within 30 seconds. It is not shown or copied again.

title: See your agent tokens
summary: Lists the live agent tokens: the label, the node, what each may do now, when it expires and when it was last used. The list never shows a token itself; the broker keeps only a hash. If you narrow a node's agent access, its tokens narrow at once.
where: App: Settings > Agents > Agent tokens. CLI: credmgr agent token ls [--node <id>]
steps: Open Settings > Agents, or run credmgr agent token ls.

title: Replace an agent token

title: Touch ID
summary: Touch ID confirms the sensitive things: creating a grant, moving a project, the full audit record, showing a 2FA seed, widening a node's reach, rotating the root key, rebuilding the registry, and opening a sealed (Orphaned) entry, and approving an AI assistant's waiting request from an open vault (denying never asks). Each asks the Secure Enclave to sign a one-time challenge, so a fingerprint (or the Mac password) is needed every time; nothing is remembered. Adding a key proves it: the new key signs a one-time challenge too, so a second fingerprint is asked for when you set it up. The list of keys is kept inside the vault's signed registry, so deleting or replacing a file in the vault folder does not remove a key or bring an old one back. On a Mac without a Secure Enclave the row is shown greyed out, with the reason, instead of being hidden.

title: Machine lock: lock the vault to this Mac
summary: Seals the vault's passphrase file with a device key kept on this Mac, outside the vault folder (a file only your user account can read), and replaces the root key and every project key at the same time. A copy of the vault folder made from then on - a synced folder, a copied directory, a USB disk - does not open on another computer with the passphrase alone. A copy made before still opens with the passphrase and still shows what it held then; nothing written after the lock is readable in it. Turning it on asks for the passphrase and your current recovery code, then shows you a NEW recovery code and asks you to type it back before anything changes; only then is the lock turned on, and the old code stops working. Closing the dialog before that changes nothing. On a new Mac, on another Mac that shares the folder, or if the key file is lost, open the vault with the recovery code; that also locks it to that Mac. It does not protect a stolen or unlocked Mac, Time Machine, a whole-disk image or Migration Assistant (they carry the device key with the folder), or CredMgr backups (they hold the passphrase file unsealed inside their own encryption and open with their backup passphrase and the vault passphrase; while the lock is on they are written outside the vault folder, in CredMgr's state folder on this Mac, and turning it on moves the ones already in the vault folder there, so a copy of the vault folder does not carry them). The key is a file, not sealed in the Secure Enclave. Rotating the root key and changing the passphrase keep the lock on, and say so if they could not.
where: App: Settings > Security > Machine lock > Bind. CLI: credmgr keystore bind
steps: Have your passphrase and your current recovery code ready, and unlock every project.
Open Settings > Security and choose Bind on the Machine lock row.
Read what it covers and what it does not, type the passphrase and the recovery code, then choose Next. Nothing has changed yet.

Also says what the lock protects (a copy of the vault folder made after it) and what it does not (a stolen or unlocked Mac, Time Machine and disk images, copies made before it, CredMgr backups, or whoever holds the recovery code). Needs the owner's login; an agent is refused.
where: App: Settings > Security > Machine lock. CLI: credmgr keystore status
steps: Open Settings > Security and read the Machine lock row, or run credmgr keystore status.

title: Turn off the machine lock

title: Unlock with Touch ID

The vault key is sealed in this Mac's Secure Enclave and opens only on this Mac, with your fingerprint or the Mac password. Your passphrase and recovery code keep working, and a second factor, if on, is still asked. The Touch ID dialog says which program asked and from which folder (for example "Unlock CredMgr for credmgr (pid 4021) <- zsh <- Terminal, in ~/projects/app"): cancel any request you did not start. title: Approve or deny an assistant's request
summary: Approving a change that weakens the vault asks you to confirm it is you first (Touch ID or your passphrase). Denying changes nothing.
where: Settings, Agents (the app). CLI: credmgr settings approve <id> | credmgr settings deny <id>.
steps: Read the request: what changes, from what to what, and why.
Approve (confirm with Touch ID or your passphrase) or deny.

title: The knowledge base for AI assistants
summary: docs/LLM_KB.md tells an assistant everything it needs: how to connect, where data lives, retention and backup, every feature and setting and how to change it, and the rules. It is generated from the settings table and checked against it, so it cannot drift.
where: File: v2/docs/LLM_KB.md. CLI: credmgr kb. MCP: credmgr_kb.
steps: Ask your assistant to read CredMgr's knowledge base (credmgr_kb), or run credmgr kb.

title: Tags on an entry
summary: An entry can carry up to 16 tags: short labels such as prod or team:payments. A tag is lower-cased and its spaces become '-'. Tags are read like names: you can list one project by a tag, but a tag never finds entries across projects. Only you set them; no agent can.
where: App: entry detail > the tag box under the name. CLI: credmgr tag <name> --add <tag>, credmgr list --node <id> --tag <tag>
steps: In the app, open the entry, type a tag in the box under its name and press Enter; the x on a tag removes it.
On the command line, run credmgr tag stripe --node acme --add prod, then credmgr list --node acme --tag prod.

title: Merge suggestions
summary: Lists entries inside one project that look like one thing: identical values, a value in common, or names one letter apart. Values are compared inside the broker and never shown. Each suggestion names the entry it would keep (the oldest).
where: App: Tidy up > Merge / Dismiss. CLI: credmgr merge suggest --node <id>
steps: On the command line, run credmgr merge suggest --node acme.
In the app, open Tidy up: copies inside one project offer Merge and Dismiss.

title: Merge duplicate entries
summary: Keeps one entry and folds the others into it: their names become its other names (aliases), their tags join its tags, and they are removed. Each removed entry can be brought back for 7 days with undo, under its own name. Needs a fresh second-factor code when one is set up.
where: App: Tidy up > Merge / Dismiss. CLI: credmgr merge apply --node <id> --keep <name> --drop <name>
steps: Run credmgr merge apply --node acme --keep STRIPE_KEY --drop stripe-key.
To take it back, run the credmgr undo line it prints.

title: Merge one identical group
summary: Merges one suggestion by its key, but only when every entry in it holds exactly the same values, so nothing is lost; it keeps the oldest entry.
where: App: Tidy up > Merge / Dismiss. CLI: credmgr merge auto --node <id> --group <key>
steps: Run credmgr merge suggest --node acme and copy the key of an identical group.
Run credmgr merge auto --node acme --group <key>.

title: Merge every identical group
summary: Plans every identical group in a project and changes nothing; with --apply it merges them all. Groups with a grant on an entry to be removed are skipped.
where: App: Tidy up > Merge / Dismiss. CLI: credmgr merge auto-all --node <id> [--apply]
steps: Run credmgr merge auto-all --node acme to see the plan.
Run it again with --apply to merge.

title: Dismiss a merge suggestion
summary: Tells CredMgr that a suggested group is not a duplicate. The project remembers it (sealed with the project's key) and it is not suggested again.
where: App: Tidy up > Dismiss. CLI: credmgr merge dismiss --node <id> --group <key>
steps: In Tidy up, choose Dismiss on the finding.
Or run credmgr merge dismiss --node acme --group <key>.

title: Undo a dismissal
summary: Forgets one dismissed merge suggestion, so it is suggested again.
where: CLI: credmgr merge undismiss --node <id> --group <key>
steps: Run credmgr merge dismissed --node acme to find the key.
Run credmgr merge undismiss --node acme --group <key>.

title: Dismissed merge suggestions
summary: Lists the groups a project remembers as not duplicates, newest first, with their entries' names.
where: CLI: credmgr merge dismissed --node <id>
steps: Run credmgr merge dismissed --node acme.

title: Forget every dismissal
summary: Forgets every dismissed merge suggestion in a project, so they can be suggested again.
where: CLI: credmgr merge restore-all --node <id>
steps: Run credmgr merge restore-all --node acme.
